lessons.title: Passing lines
lessons.objective: Choose the passing line on the track.

payload.prompt: Tap every groove where a pass can happen.

diagram.alt: Overhead diagram of a banked turn with three painted lanes: low near the infield, middle and high next to the wall.

explanation.correct: Right. Passes can happen in any groove, depending on where the grip and the momentum are.
explanation.incorrect: All three grooves can be used for a pass. Which one is quickest changes with the track, the rubber and the tires, so drivers try different lanes.

payload.prompt: What sets up a typical pass on an oval?

options.text: A run off the draft carried into the next turn.
Lifting early so the gap to the leader grows.
Staying in the leader's dirty air all lap.

explanation.correct: Right. Extra speed from a run lets the trailing car pull alongside before the corner, which is where many passes are made.
explanation.incorrect: A pass needs extra speed or grip. A run off the draft gives the speed, while lifting or sitting in dirty air takes away the grip and the chance.

payload.prompt: Can you pass on the high groove?

scene.alt: Two cars racing side-by-side on the high groove of a turn.

explanation.correct: Right. The high line is the longer way around, but it can work for a pass if the grip and momentum are there.
explanation.incorrect: The high groove is often the longer way, but it can be used for a pass if you have momentum or if rubber has built up there.

payload.prompt: Match the groove to its role.

pairs.definition: The line closest to the infield, the shortest way around.
Between low and high; a flexible choice in traffic.
Along the wall, the longer way, but it offers room for a run.

explanation.summary: Three grooves offer three passing zones, and which one is fastest shifts as the rubber builds.

payload.prompt: Where does a draft run usually pay off?
payload.template: A run from the draft usually pays off at {{place}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The extra speed from a run lets the trailing car get alongside into the turn, which is where many passes happen.
explanation.incorrect: The speed from a draft run pays off at turn entry, where the trailing car can pull alongside the leader before the corner.

lessons.title: Restart lane and jump
lessons.objective: Pick the restart lane and gain spots on the jump.

configuration.prompt: Green restart: inside or outside? Choose and watch the lanes.
configuration.setup: Caution restart: pick inside (safe) or outside (risky). See how both lanes stack on the restart.

payload.prompt: What is a good jump on a restart?

options.text: Accelerating as the green drops, without beating the leader to the line.
Launching early, before the restart zone.
Waiting for the car behind to go first.

explanation.correct: Right. A good jump is getting up to speed right as the green drops. Going too early can bring a restart penalty.
explanation.incorrect: The skill is timing. You want to launch as the leader does and as the green drops, not before the restart zone and not late enough to be passed.

payload.prompt: Under the choose rule, does the leader pick a lane first?

scene.alt: Restart lineup with two lanes and the leader at the front.

explanation.correct: Right. Drivers choose in running order, so the leader picks inside or outside first and the cars behind follow.
explanation.incorrect: The choose rule follows the running order, so the leader has first choice of lane. That is a real reward for running in front.

payload.prompt: You restart second and the leader took the inside. Which lane?

situation.narrative: The leader chose the inside. You are next in the running order with a choice of lane.

facts.label: Tires
facts.value: Both of you on fresh tires

facts.label: Earlier restarts
facts.value: The outside lane got the better run

options.label: Take the outside lane
options.consequence: You line up beside the leader in the lane that has been getting the better run, so you can launch on the same terms and threaten the lead.
considerations: Earlier restarts showed the outside had the run.
With 45 to go there is time to recover if it goes wrong.
You stay next to the leader, not behind him.

options.label: Take the inside lane behind him
options.consequence: You are safe and tucked in, but you start in the lane that has been slower and behind the leader.
considerations: You give up the lane with the better run.
It costs you a shot at the lead.

payload.expertNote: Lane choice is a read of the track, not a dare. Crew chiefs and spotters look at how the lanes have behaved all day.

lessons.title: Getting clean air
lessons.objective: Explain how to pass in clean air.

payload.prompt: Can you pass in dirty air?

scene.alt: Follower in dirty air trying to pass the leader.

explanation.correct: Right. Dirty air makes passing hard, but not impossible. You need more speed or ideal conditions.
explanation.incorrect: You can pass in dirty air if your car is faster, but dirty air reduces grip and makes passes very difficult. Most clean-air passes happen when the trailing car exits dirty air.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: Once I got clean air, I had a shot.

options.text: Out of disturbed air behind the leader, I had grip to pass.
The weather cleared and the driver raced harder.
When the pit crew fixed the air vents.

payload.translation: When I moved out of disturbed air, my car had grip to attempt a pass.

followUps.line: Clean air gives front grip because no car disrupts the airflow.
followUps.why: Aerodynamics decide whether a pass is even possible.

followUps.line: Clean-air passes often happen three-wide when the inside car clears.
followUps.why: Once you have grip, you can turn and dive to a different line.

payload.prompt: What does dirty air do?

options.text: It slows the engine by restricting intake airflow.
It reduces front grip and makes the car pushy.
It creates a slipstream that speeds up the car.

explanation.correct: Right. Dirty air reduces front grip, making you push (understeer) and turn poorly.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air disrupts airflow over your splitter and nose, reducing downforce and front grip. You push and cannot turn.

payload.prompt: A clean-air pass is easiest when {{condition}}.
payload.template: A clean-air pass is easiest when {{condition}}.

options: the trailing car exits dirty air
gaps.correct: the trailing car exits dirty air

explanation.correct: Right. Exiting dirty air suddenly gives grip. That is the moment to attack.
explanation.incorrect: A pass occurs when the trailing car moves from dirty to clean air and gains grip. That grip delta opens the passing window.

lessons.title: Blocking and being blocked
lessons.objective: Judge whether a block is legal.

payload.prompt: Is blocking a legal move?

scene.alt: Two cars, one moving to block the other.

explanation.correct: Right. One block per attempt is legal and expected. Repeated blocks anger rivals.
explanation.incorrect: Blocking is legal. A leading car can move once to defend. Multiple blocks or very late blocks may be penalized or draw retaliation.

payload.prompt: He blocks low, you go high, he goes high. What now?

options.label: Accept and wait.
options.consequence: Clean racing, you earn respect, but lose this battle.
considerations: But you might not get another chance.

options.label: Bump him off his line.
options.consequence: Fair payback for repeated blocks. He loses momentum and you dive past.

options.label: Wreck him.
options.consequence: Both of you DNF. Not worth 8 laps.

payload.expertNote: Repeated blocking—moving back and forth—crosses from defense into aggression and invites retaliation.

payload.prompt: Match the block type to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A single move to defend your line; legal and expected.
Moving back-and-forth to defend; can be penalized or provoke retaliation.
Blocking at the last moment; often dirty and draws anger.

explanation.summary: One block is racing. Multiple blocks are not and earn a dirty reputation.

payload.prompt: When is a block penalized?

options.text: Every time you defend your line.
For repeated or very late blocks.
Never; blocks are always legal.

explanation.correct: Right. One block is clean. Multiple blocks or a very late block may be flagged.
explanation.incorrect: Blocking is legal, but excessive blocking or blocking very late into the corner may draw a penalty. The line between racing and wrecking matters.

payload.prompt: Where is the braking zone? Tap the area.

image.alt: Road-course turn with approach, braking zone and apex.

options.text: Straight approach
options.explanation: You are at full throttle here; braking has not started.

options.text: Braking zone
options.explanation: The braking zone is where drivers slow down. A pass often happens here (out-braking).

options.text: Apex (turn center)
options.explanation: The apex is too late; the pass must happen on entry, in the braking zone.

explanation.correct: Right. Passes on road courses often happen in the braking zone, where the trailing car out-brakes the leader.
explanation.incorrect: Passes on a road course happen in the braking zone, where the trailing car out-brakes the leader and gains inside position.

payload.prompt: What is key to passing on a road course?

options.text: Out-braking into the corner and diving inside.
Drafting down the straightaway.
Having higher top speed.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A road-course pass is about braking: out-brake the leader into a corner and take the inside line. Skill and patience win.
explanation.incorrect: Road-course racing is about braking precision. A trailing car passes by braking later, diving inside and carrying more speed through the apex.

payload.prompt: You brake better. Dive for the inside?

options.label: Dive inside in braking zone.
options.consequence: Out-braking the leader gains inside position. If you nail the turn, you are past. Road-course passing is about braking.

options.label: Wait for a mistake.
options.consequence: Conservative. You might never get a cleaner shot.

payload.expertNote: Road-course specialists pass in the braking zone. Out-braking is how passes happen when skill separates drivers.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: I out-braked him into the chicane.

options.text: I braked later than he did, diving inside the quick left-right section.
I used better brakes than he had.
I forced his brakes to fail.

payload.translation: I braked later than the leader, gaining inside position into the chicane.

followUps.line: Out-braking means braking later than your rival; it is the signature road-course pass.
followUps.why: On road courses, braking point is where passes are made.

followUps.line: A failed out-braking attempt can result in a crash at the apex if you run out of room.
followUps.why: Road-course racecraft is about knowing the limit and executing perfectly.

lessons.title: Lapped traffic
lessons.objective: Explain how lapped cars affect racing.

payload.prompt: You are fourth; lapped car is in your way. Pass it?

facts.label: Traffic
facts.value: Lapped car is in the way

options.label: Pass the lapped car.
options.consequence: Overtaking clears your line and lets you chase third.

options.label: Wait for it to clear.
options.consequence: The car might yield. You save fuel and tires.

payload.expertNote: Lapped traffic is a hazard for leaders but a tool for others; passing or using them can change the race.

payload.prompt: What does 'a lap down' mean?

options.text: One fewer lap than the leader, out of contention.
Three seconds behind the leader.
Still has pit stops remaining.

explanation.correct: Right. A lapped car has one full lap fewer than the leader. Out of contention but still racing.
explanation.incorrect: Being a lap down means the leader has lapped you—you are one full lap behind. Still racing, but cannot win unless the leader crashes or pits late.

payload.prompt: Can lapped traffic help a chasing driver?

scene.alt: Leader slowing for lapped car while chaser runs free.

choices.label: Yes, it can slow the leader.
No, it only hurts the chaser.

explanation.correct: Yes. Lapped traffic might slow the leader more than the chaser, closing the gap.
explanation.incorrect: Lapped traffic usually hurts the leader more than a chaser who can navigate around it better. Smart drivers use traffic to gain time.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: We got held up by traffic.

options.text: Slower, lapped cars blocked our path and cost us speed.
The pit crew was stuck in the stall.
Road construction delayed the race start.

payload.translation: We had to navigate around or slow for lapped cars in our way.

followUps.line: Lapped traffic is both a hazard and a factor; it can help or hurt depending on who is faster.
followUps.why: On a restart, lapped cars can shuffle the running order.

followUps.line: Free passes and wave-arounds manage lapped car disruption and keep racing close.
followUps.why: Letting a lapped car get back on the lead lap reduces frustration.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: He will get some payback for that.

options.text: He will face retaliation on track in a future race.
He will receive a financial refund.
He will be fined by NASCAR.

payload.translation: He will face retaliation or a bump if he crossed the line; it is part of the driver code.

followUps.line: Payback is a NASCAR tradition; if you wreck someone or block dirty, expect a bump later.
followUps.why: Drivers police themselves and each other on track. Respect and consequences shape behavior.

followUps.line: Payback does not have to be a wreck; it can be a bump, blocking, or passing that costs position.
followUps.why: There is a spectrum from clean racing to dirty; payback can stay within that spectrum.

payload.title: She expects payback
payload.setting: After a wreck caused by her driver's rival.

exchanges.theirMessage: He just wrecked my guy. Next race, he is getting a bump.

replies.text: Do you think that settles it, or does it keep going?
replies.theirResponse: Depends on what the bump does. If it is clean, maybe.
replies.coachNote: You acknowledged payback and asked if it ends the feud.

replies.theirResponse: It is, but I hope he understands.
replies.coachNote: Empathy is good, but ask about the outcome.

replies.text: That is just how it is.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, but nobody wants it out of hand.
replies.coachNote: True, but show you get the stakes.

payload.closingNote: Payback is tradition, but drivers also know when to let it go.

payload.prompt: Is payback the same as a wreck?

scene.alt: Two-car contact showing a bump vs a crash.

explanation.correct: Right. Payback is retaliation, but does not have to be a wreck. A bump, block or pass can be payback.
explanation.incorrect: Payback is the tradition of responding to a wrong, but it does not always mean wrecking. A bump that costs position, a block, or beating someone fair can all be payback.

payload.prompt: He wrecked you last week. He is now behind you. Wreck him?

facts.label: What happened
facts.value: He dumped you last week at race end

facts.label: Today
facts.value: He is in sixth, you are fourth

facts.label: Points
facts.value: You are close; a DNF hurts

options.label: Race him clean and beat him.
options.consequence: You earn respect and keep racing. A clean win is better. You can race him later.

options.label: Bump him if he tries to pass.
options.consequence: Fair payback. You cost him track position. He gets the message.

options.label: Wreck him like he wrecked you.
options.consequence: You might both DNF. You now look like the dirty driver. Feuds escalate.
considerations: Feuds escalate when you trade wrecks.

payload.expertNote: Payback is tradition, but wreck-for-wreck turns a grudge into a feud. Smart racers respond with a bump or a clean beat, then move on.

lessons.title: Racing vs wrecking
lessons.objective: Judge whether contact is racing or wrecking.

payload.prompt: Is all contact in NASCAR wrecking?

scene.alt: Controlled bump vs hard crash side-by-side.

explanation.correct: Right. A bump or controlled contact is racing. A wreck is reckless contact that destroys a car.
explanation.incorrect: Contact happens in close racing. A bump to move someone or slight tap to pass is racing. A wreck is when someone loses control or a car is heavily damaged.

options.text: The contact was aggressive but within bounds of racing.
The car broke down due to engine trouble.
The pit crew worked very hard.

payload.translation: The bump or contact was aggressive but not malicious; it is part of the sport.

followUps.line: Hard racing includes bumps, tight passes and defensive moves that do not ruin a car.
followUps.why: Drivers accept some contact as the cost of trying to pass or defend position.

followUps.line: Wrecking is when the contact is reckless, intentional or ends in a crash; fans and drivers draw that line.
followUps.why: The culture polices itself: wreck someone and payback or a bad reputation follows.

payload.prompt: Match the contact type to what it is.

pairs.definition: Aggressive contact: bumps, blocks and tight passes within the bounds of the sport.
Reckless or intentional contact that destroys a car or ends a race.
Deliberately crashing another driver; penalized and draws fines or suspensions.

distractorDefinitions: Losing grip and sliding off track.

explanation.summary: Racing and wrecking are separated by intent and outcome. A bump is racing; a hard crash is wrecking.

payload.prompt: He defends, you both slide. Racing or wrecking?

facts.label: The move
facts.value: You pass low, he defends low

options.label: That was racing.
options.consequence: Clean battle. No one wrecked; you both knew the risk.

options.label: He wrecked you.
options.consequence: He defended his line. If you complain to NASCAR, they will laugh.
considerations: Sliding is part of the game.

payload.expertNote: Racing means everyone knows the risk. If you commit to a pass and the driver defends, slides happen and that is racing.
